# Day 7: Protein Structure

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to describe the four
levels of protein structure, use PyMOL to load and inspect a real
structure, and explain why predicting the tertiary (3D) fold from
sequence alone is a harder problem than the secondary-structure
prediction Day 6 already introduced.

## The four levels of protein structure

A protein starts as a **polypeptide chain**: a linear polymer of amino
acids, connected head-to-tail, that only becomes a functional protein
once it folds up in water. Structural biology describes that folded
result at four increasingly complex levels:

- **Primary structure** — the sequence of amino acids itself, exactly
  the object Days 1-6 have been aligning, scoring, and classifying. No
  3D information yet.
- **Secondary structure** — local, repeating backbone shapes, already
  introduced narratively on Day 6: the **alpha helix**, a coil held
  together by hydrogen bonds between backbone N-H and C=O groups four
  residues apart, and the **beta sheet**, built from extended **beta
  strands** hydrogen-bonded edge to edge with their neighbors. Anything
  that's neither is usually just called **coil**.
- **Tertiary structure** — how those secondary-structure elements, and
  everything connecting them, pack together into one compact 3D shape
  for a single chain. This is held together mostly by the
  **hydrophobic effect** (water excludes non-polar side chains from its
  surface, driving them to bury themselves inside the fold) plus
  weaker non-covalent forces between atoms of the backbone and side
  chains (hydrogen bonds, electrostatic attraction between charged side
  chains, and van der Waals contacts).
- **Quaternary structure** — how multiple, separately-folded chains
  arrange themselves with respect to each other into one functional
  assembly. Not every protein has this level at all (many function as
  a single chain); those that do can range from two chains up to,
  in some experimentally solved structures, hundreds.

**A real example, continuing this course's running case study.**
Hemoglobin is a **heterotetramer**: two copies of an alpha-globin chain
(141 residues) and two copies of *HBB*, beta-globin (146 residues, this
course's running example since Day 3), each chain independently folded
and each carrying its own oxygen-binding heme group. The notebook
re-derives — independently of Day 6's PDBe API lookup, using a different
tool (PyMOL's own `dss` algorithm) — that one beta chain is **118 of 146
residues (80.8%) alpha helix, 0% beta strand**, confirming Day 6's number
by a second, unrelated computational method rather than just repeating
it. Rendering all four chains together, colored separately, with the
four hemes shown as spheres, makes tertiary and quaternary structure
directly visible at once:

![PDB entry `2HHB`, human deoxyhemoglobin: two alpha chains (blue/cyan),
two beta chains (salmon/pink), four heme iron atoms (orange spheres).
Rendered from the real structure with PyMOL, not
illustrated.](figs/day07-hemoglobin-tetramer.png){width=85%}

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Protein structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_structure) — a fuller treatment of all four levels
- RCSB [PDB-101](https://pdb101.rcsb.org/) — short, illustrated explainers on structure and specific proteins, aimed at newcomers

## Why predicting the fold from sequence is hard

A given amino acid sequence reliably folds into the same 3D structure
every time under normal cellular conditions — this observation is often
called **Anfinsen's dogma**, after Christian Anfinsen's experiments
showing a denatured (unfolded) protein could refold correctly entirely on
its own, with no other machinery needed. That implies all the
information needed to determine the fold is, in principle, already
present in the sequence.

In principle is the operative phrase: reliably *predicting* that fold
computationally, starting from sequence alone, has been one of
biology's hardest open problems for decades. Three classical strategies
were developed, each with a real limitation:

- **De novo (ab initio) modeling** — simulate the physics directly:
  fold the chain by searching for the arrangement with the lowest free
  energy. The most rigorous approach in principle, but computationally
  so expensive it was, for a long time, only practical for small
  proteins (under roughly 100 residues).
- **Comparative modeling (homology modeling / threading)** — if a
  protein of known structure is similar enough in sequence, assume the
  new protein folds the same way and build a model from that template.
  Cheap and reliable when a good template exists, but structurally
  useless for a genuinely new fold with no close relative already
  solved.
- **Evolutionary (contact-based) methods** — infer which residue pairs
  are likely to be physically close in the folded structure from
  patterns of co-evolution across many homologous sequences in a
  multiple alignment. This is the same evolutionary information Day 5's
  profiles and PSSMs are built from, now used for a 3D geometric
  question rather than a purely sequence-based score — a second,
  independent instance of "evolutionary information helps," one level up
  in structural complexity from Day 6's secondary-structure example.

None of these three classical strategies solved the general problem
reliably. The real breakthrough came from a fourth strategy — deep
learning, most famously AlphaFold (2020) — which Day 12 covers properly,
once this course has built up the neural-network machinery (Days 6-9)
that made it possible.

Structures also need to be **compared** to each other quantitatively,
not just predicted — e.g. to check how close a predicted structure is to
the real one. The most common such measure, root-mean-square deviation
(RMSD) between corresponding atoms after optimally superimposing the two
structures, and a length-independent alternative, the TM-score, are
outside this session's scope but worth knowing exist.

- Wikipedia, [Anfinsen's dogma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anfinsen%27s_dogma)

- Wikipedia, [Root-mean-square deviation of atomic positions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root-mean-square_deviation_of_atomic_positions) and [Template modeling score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template_modeling_score) — the two most common structure-comparison measures, not needed until they come up again with AlphaFold on Day 12

## Structure visualization: PyMOL

[PyMOL](https://pymol.org/) is one of the two most widely used molecular
visualization programs in structural biology (alongside ChimeraX),
free and open-source. It loads a structure directly from a PDB entry,
renders it in several standard representations — **cartoon** (secondary
structure as ribbons/arrows/coils, used for the figure above), **sticks**
(every bond drawn explicitly, useful for a single side chain or ligand),
and **spheres** (every atom as a ball, useful for packing/space-filling
views) — and can measure real geometric quantities (distances, angles)
directly from the loaded coordinates by clicking on atoms or via its
command line. Today's lab uses it hands-on; the notebook drives the same
program headlessly from Python to make its figures and measurements
reproducible outside the interactive GUI.

## The notebook

`notebooks/day07-protein-structure-in-code.ipynb` fetches two real
hemoglobin structures — deoxygenated `2HHB` and oxygenated `1HHO` — and
uses them to make every level of structure concrete: primary and
quaternary structure from simply parsing chains, secondary structure
independently cross-checked against Day 6's number using PyMOL's own
algorithm, and a real measured quaternary-structure distance (the
iron-to-iron distance between the two beta hemes) that changes by about
5 Å between the two states — a genuine, measured instance of
hemoglobin's textbook allosteric mechanism (Baldwin & Chothia, 1979), not
just a diagram. Open it in
[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/day07-protein-structure-in-code.ipynb)
via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it
yourself.

## The lab

**Full lab, PyMOL-first:** load hemoglobin (PDB `2HHB`, continuing the
*HBB* thread from Days 3 and 6) directly in PyMOL, use its cartoon
representation to identify the same alpha helices Day 6 already
quantified from the PDBe API, and use PyMOL's built-in distance
measurement to reproduce, hands-on in the GUI, the beta-beta heme
iron-to-iron distance the notebook computes in code — then compare it
against the oxygenated structure (`1HHO`) to see the same allosteric
shift found in the notebook.

## What's next

Day 8 moves from a single yes/no output (Day 6's XOR problem) to
multi-class prediction — softmax regression — and from raw
tensors to a properly structured PyTorch model, using a real multi-class
biological problem (subcellular localization) as the case study. Day 9
comes back to deliver Rost & Sander's PHD method in full, now that both
the hidden-layer motivation (Day 6) and the tools to build one properly
(Day 8) are in place.
